extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and translators of Old English poetry (Beowulf); editors of medieval texts
extracted.subtask_description: Close translation and editorial commentary on Old English Beowulf lines, including emendation, punctuation, and lexical decisions. Aimed at producing an annotated, coherent modern-English rendering and textual apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammatical function and naturalness of contested words (e.g., 'unforhte' 444)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Unforhte' (444) is much disputed.--H.-So. wavers between adj. and adv. Gr. and B. take it as an adv. modifying etan: Will eat the Geats fearlessly.--Kl. considers this reading absurd, and proposes 'anforhte' = timid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether a contested form is adjective or adverb by weighing syntactic fit, naturalness of the resulting phrase, and prosodic/parallel structures (e.g., taking 'unforhte' as an adj. gives a parallel to 'Geátena leóde', but as an adv. is more natural). Also consider interpretive consequences (e.g., whether calling the Geats 'brave' implies an unintended thrust at the Danes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh alternative translations for tonal effect (literal vs. idiomatic) (e.g., 'head-watch')
rubrics_metrics.description: For 'head-watch,' cf. H.-So. notes and cf. v. 2910.--Th. translates: 'Thou wilt not need my head to hide' (i.e., thou wilt have no occasion to bury me, as Grendel will devour me whole).--Simrock imagines a kind of dead-watch.--Dr. H. Wood suggests: 'Thou wilt not have to bury so much as my head' (for Grendel will be a thorough undertaker),--grim humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a rendering that conveys the intended tone (grim humor, literal threat, ironic understatement). Balance literal word-for-word translation against idiomatic English that preserves rhetorical effect and register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat ambiguous lexical items cautiously (e.g., 'feorme', 'líc')
rubrics_metrics.description: Owing to the vagueness of 'feorme' (451), this passage is variously translated. ... 'Líc' is also a crux here, as it may mean living body or dead body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a word has multiple plausible senses, record possibilities in the apparatus or glossary, choose the sense best supported by context and parallel usage, and indicate uncertainty in notes. Compare authoritative glossaries and existing translations before committing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use punctuation and sentence-division as interpretive devices
rubrics_metrics.description: S. proposes a colon after 'nimeð' (l. 447). This would make no essential change in the translation. Kl. suggests a period after 'determined.' This would give the passage as follows: ... All the renderings are unsatisfactory, the one given in our translation involving a zeugma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that punctuation/emendation (commas, colons, periods) can change clause connections, create or remove zeugma, and affect clarity. State punctuation choices in commentary and justify them by showing how they alter meaning or syntactic coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emendation to improve coherence and motive (editorial reconstruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: B. and S. reject the reading given in H.-So., and suggested by Grtvg. B. suggests for 457-458: 'wáere-ryhtum Þú, wine mín Béowulf, and for ár-stafum úsic sóhtest.' This means: 'From the obligations of clientage, my friend Beowulf, and for assistance thou hast sought us'.--This gives coherence to Hrothgar's opening remarks in VIII., and also introduces a new motive for Beowulf's coming to Hrothgar's aid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may propose emendations when manuscript readings yield incoherence or obscure motive. Emendations should be justified by improved syntactic or semantic coherence, parallels elsewhere in the text, and philological plausibility; variants and rationale must be recorded in the apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow and cite authoritative glossaries/translations where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: In our translation, H.-So.'s glossary has been quite closely followed. This agrees substantially with B.'s translation (P. and B. XII. 87). R. translates: 'Thou needst not take care longer as to the consumption of my dead body.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established glossaries and prior reputable translations for difficult words or phrases; note agreements and departures. Explicitly cite the sources followed to justify lexical choices and to aid readers in comparing interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider morphological/lexical alternatives that alter clause function (e.g., 'síð' meaning 'arrival')
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been plausibly suggested that 'síð' (in 501 and in 353) means 'arrival.' If so, translate the bracket: '(the arrival of Beowulf, the brave seafarer, was a source of great chagrin to Unferth, etc.)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate glosses for single words may change the syntactic role of clauses (e.g., noun vs. verb readings). Evaluate morphological possibilities and show in notes how alternative readings shift the translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve or explicate poetic/formal features where relevant (alliteration, measure, rhetorical figures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The gleeman sang whilom ... 'gan then Beowulf's venture' ... 'Wisely to tell of, and words that were clever / To utter skilfully, earnestly speaking' — the text remarks on alliterative measures and rhythmic craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating verse, decide whether to attempt to preserve poetic features (alliteration, meter, rhetorical devices) or to prioritize sense and readability. State the approach taken and provide glosses or literal notes when poetic effects are sacrificed for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record variant readings and scholarly opinions in the apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous notes cite readings and emendations by H.-So., Gr., B., Kl., Th., Simrock, Dr. H. Wood, R., S., etc., and frequently say 'B. suggests', 'Kl. suggests', 'S. emends', 't.B. accepts'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a clear textual apparatus that lists variant manuscript readings, proposed emendations, and competing scholarly interpretations. Give concise justification for the preferred reading and cross-reference parallels and earlier editors' arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid interpretive choices that introduce unintended sociopolitical implications
rubrics_metrics.description: To call the Geats 'brave' might, at this point, seem like an implied thrust at the Danes, so long helpless; while to call his own men 'timid' would befouling his own nest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert that lexical choices may carry intergroup or political connotations in the source culture or for modern readers. Weigh whether a given rendering inadvertently casts characters or groups in a light that contradicts authorial nuance; note such risks in commentary and, if necessary, provide alternative translations or explanatory notes.
